T≤D+1 in ℝ≥0∞, for D=dimH(E) in Euclidean Rn(n₀) and T=dimH(F) in the maximum product metric. Both dimensions are finite, and this is equivalently the inequality between their nonnegative real representatives.

0≤D≤n₀<∞ and 1≤T≤n₀+1<∞, where D=dimH(E) in Euclidean Rn(n₀) and T=dimH(F) in MaxProd(Rn(n₀)). Also dimH(I)=1. In particular D and T have finite nonnegative real representatives, and their orders and addition by finite numbers agree with the corresponding ℝ≥0∞ operations. These assertions include n₀=0.

T=D+1, where D=dimH(E) in Euclidean Rn(n₀) and T=dimH(F) in MaxProd(Rn(n₀)). Both sides are finite extended nonnegative reals. Equivalently, dimH(E×I)=dimH(E)+1 in the maximum product metric, for the original nonempty compact E and every natural n₀, including n₀=0.

The coordinate concatenation map j(n₀):L2Prod(n₀)→Rn(n₀+1) is a bijective isometry for the library L² product norm and the Euclidean norm on Rn(n₀+1). Its inverse truncates the first n₀ coordinates and extracts the last coordinate. It sends euclideanLift n₀ '' F exactly to G. For any x,y∈Rn(n₀) and t,u∈ℝ, the squared distance of the concatenated points is Σ_{h<n₀}|x_h-y_h|²+|t-u|², equal to the squared L² product distance between euclideanLift n₀ (x,t) and euclideanLift n₀ (y,u). For n₀=0 the sum is empty and this is the usual identification of ℝ^0×ℝ with ℝ.

dimH(G)=dimH(E)+1, where E has its original Euclidean metric and G is E×[0,1] identified with Euclidean Rn(n₀+1) as specified in the selected target; this holds for every natural n₀, including n₀=0. Both sides are finite, so the equality also holds for real Hausdorff dimensions.

The n₀ coordinate unit vectors form a real basis of Rn(n₀): every vector is its finite coordinate linear combination, and equality of coordinates forces all coefficients in a zero combination to vanish. There are n₀ vectors. For n₀=0 this is the empty basis of the zero vector space. In MaxProd(Rn(n₀)), the n₀ vectors (e_h,0) together with (0,1) similarly span uniquely, by the first coordinates and last coordinate, so its real dimension is n₀+1. Both are real normed vector spaces (the second with the maximum product norm) and finite dimensional. Apply M007 to their full spaces and M006 to E⊆univ Rn(n₀) and F⊆univ MaxProd(Rn(n₀)). We obtain 0≤D≤n₀ and 0≤T≤n₀+1. The lower zero bounds follow from the ℝ≥0∞ codomain of dimH. Thus D and T are finite, including when n₀=0. A finite extended nonnegative real is the cast of its unique nonnegative real representative, and casts preserve finite sums and order.
0≤D≤n₀<∞ and 0≤T≤n₀+1<∞; both dimensions have nonnegative real representatives with the same finite order and addition.
f_f:ℝ→MaxProd(Rn(n₀)) is an isometry and f_f '' I⊆F.

Apply M008 to f_f and I, using the isometry in F003. It gives dimH(f_f '' I)=dimH(I)=1 by F002. Apply M006 to f_f '' I⊆F, also in F003, to get 1≤dimH(F)=T. Combining with F001 proves 0≤D≤n₀<∞ and 1≤T≤n₀+1<∞, together with dimH(I)=1 and the finite real identifications. The chosen point and its map do not occur in N004.
S001 displays bases of size n₀ and n₀+1, including the empty basis for Rn(0).
Take W=Rn(n₀), A=E,B=univ; then W=MaxProd(Rn(n₀)), A=F,B=univ.
Take W=ℝ, Z=MaxProd(Rn(n₀)), f=f_f and A=I.
Take W=MaxProd(Rn(n₀)), A=f_f '' I and B=F.

Fix arbitrary real q and assume L1: q>d_real. F001 gives q>0, so q defines a nonnegative real exponent. M003 with set E and exponent q gives H^q(E)=0, since dimH(E)=D<q. Apply N002 to X=Rn(n₀), A=E and q. Its positive-exponent and zero-measure premises have just been established, and E×I in MaxProd(Rn(n₀)) is F. Therefore H^(q+1)(F)=0.

Assume for contradiction L2: k_real>d_real+1. Put q_mid=(d_real+k_real-1)/2. Then d_real<q_mid<k_real-1, because k_real-1>d_real. F003 with q=q_mid gives k_real≤q_mid+1<k_real, a contradiction. Discharge L2 to obtain k_real≤d_real+1. Cast back by F001: T≤D+1. Finiteness is already supplied by N004. This proves N005 for every natural n₀, including zero.
Take W=Rn(n₀) with its Borel structure, A=E and source nonnegative exponent d equal to q.
Rn(n₀) is a Euclidean metric space and is equipped with its Borel structure.
Take W=MaxProd(Rn(n₀)) with its Borel structure, A=F and source exponent d=q+1.

By F002, M002 applied to E at the nonnegative exponent s_mid gives H^s_mid(E)=∞, because dimH(E)=D is the cast of d_real. N003, applied with X=Rn(n₀), A=E and s=s_mid, gives H^s_mid(E)≤H^(s_mid+1)(F). Consequently H^(s_mid+1)(F)=∞. M005 with A=F and nonnegative exponent s_mid+1 yields s_mid+1≤T, equivalently s_mid+1≤k_real by F001. This contradicts F002. Discharge L2 and conclude k_real≥d_real+1 under L1. Discharge L1, and combine with the d_real=0 implication in F001 by exhaustive cases on d_real≥0. Hence k_real≥d_real+1 for all cases.

F003 gives T≥D+1, and N005 gives T≤D+1. Antisymmetry proves T=D+1. Both dimensions and their sum are finite by F001 and N004. When n₀=0, N004 forces D=0 and the fibre branch already supplies the lower bound; the upper proof also covered this case. This proves N006. Compactness remains an original hypothesis in the global specification, although this replacement proof does not use it.
Take W=Rn(n₀) with its Borel structure, A=E, and the nonnegative exponent d=s_mid.
Rn(n₀) is Euclidean and equipped with its Borel structure.
Take W=MaxProd(Rn(n₀)) with its Borel structure, A=F and exponent d=s_mid+1.

Apply the exact prepared basis port E001 to the current natural number n₀ and S=F⊆MaxProd(Rn(n₀)). It gives dimH(euclideanLift n₀ '' F)=dimH(F)=T. The port is the maximum-to-L² product dimension adapter; its underlying map is the identity on pairs, namely the inverse of WithLp.prodContinuousLinearEquiv 2 ℝ (Rn(n₀)) ℝ. The basis registry prepares this adapter from ContinuousLinearEquiv.dimH_image. We use here exactly its registered dimension equality.

N007 proves that j(n₀):L2Prod(n₀)→Rn(n₀+1) is an isometry and that j(n₀) '' (euclideanLift n₀ '' F)=G. Apply M008 with this map and set euclideanLift n₀ '' F. It gives dimH(G)=dimH(euclideanLift n₀ '' F). By F001 and N006 this equals T=D+1=dimH(E)+1. N006 also provides finiteness. By D016, G is exactly the specified Euclidean E×[0,1] under coordinate concatenation, and E on the right retains its original Euclidean Rn(n₀) metric. N007 includes the n₀=0 identification, so there is no excluded ambient dimension. Since the dimensions are finite, the extended nonnegative equality is also equality of the real Hausdorff dimensions. This is the complete selected conclusion.
Instantiate the source's natural number n₀ by the current n₀ and its set S by F=E×I in MaxProd(Rn(n₀)); its image is taken in L2Prod(n₀).
Take W=L2Prod(n₀), Z=Rn(n₀+1), f=j(n₀) and A=euclideanLift n₀ '' F.
The direct input N007 states that j(n₀) is an isometry.
For the inverse construction take any v∈Rn(n₀+1).

Fix arbitrary p,z∈L2Prod(n₀). Apply M014 with W=Rn(n₀), Z=ℝ and argument p-z. These are normed additive commutative groups, hence satisfy its seminormed assumptions. With the coordinatewise subtraction and distance as norm of difference, the source gives
 dist(p,z)²=‖p.fst-z.fst‖²+|p.snd-z.snd|²
 =Σ_{h<n₀}|p.fst_h-z.fst_h|²+|p.snd-z.snd|².
The second equality uses the defining squared Euclidean norm on Rn(n₀). On the other hand, the defining squared norm on Rn(n₀+1), split into its first n₀ coordinates and last coordinate, gives
 dist(j(n₀)(p),j(n₀)(z))²=Σ_{h<n₀}|p.fst_h-z.fst_h|²+|p.snd-z.snd|².
The two nonnegative distances have equal squares; hence they are equal. These formulas hold also when n₀=0, with an empty finite sum.
For all p,z∈L2Prod(n₀), dist(j(n₀)(p),j(n₀)(z))=dist(p,z), and their common square is Σ_{h<n₀}|p.fst_h-z.fst_h|²+|p.snd-z.snd|².

By F001, j(n₀) is an isometry. Its explicit inverse sends a vector v∈Rn(n₀+1) to the pair consisting of its first n₀ coordinates in Rn(n₀) and its last coordinate, regarded as an element of L2Prod(n₀) using euclideanLift n₀. Coordinate evaluation shows that both composites are the identity. Hence j(n₀) is bijective. By the definitions of F,G,euclideanLift and j, a point of j(n₀) '' (euclideanLift n₀ '' F) is precisely a concatenation of x∈E and t∈I; conversely every such concatenation arises this way. Thus this image equals G. Specializing F001 to p=euclideanLift n₀ (x,t) and z=euclideanLift n₀ (y,u) yields the squared-distance formula stated in N007 for every such x,y,t,u. For n₀=0 the inverse still extracts the last coordinate and the empty initial tuple; every step is unchanged.
Take the two source groups to be Rn(n₀) and ℝ and source point p equal to the current difference p-z∈L2Prod(n₀).
Rn(n₀) and ℝ are real normed additive commutative groups, hence seminormed additive commutative groups.
